t: The church is monotheistic: members believe in a supreme being, the Great Spirit or Creator, and use peyote as a sacrament that they hold to be a means of communicating with the Great Spirit.
It has two main ways, the Half-Moon way and the Cross-fire way, which differ in whether a Bible, baptism and a minister are used.
Its use of peyote came under federal drug law in 1970 and was later protected by the American Indian Religious Freedom Act of 1978 and the Religious Freedom Restoration Act of 1993.
dyk: Ceremonies are held at the request of a family, usually last all night, and end with a feast for the whole community and gifts from the sponsoring family to the Roadman and his helpers.
ev: The Oklahoma Territory period (1890–1907) in which the church originates after peyote reaches the southern Great Plains from Mexico
Victor Griffin, known as the last chief of the Quapaw, helps incorporate the Native American Church under Oklahoma law
The original charter of the Native American Church of the United States is enabled in the Oklahoma territory
James Seymour of the Winnebago introduces the Half-Moon way, in 1914 or 1924
The Native American Church is officially created
The Controlled Substances Act prohibits the possession of psychedelics such as peyote in the United States
The American Indian Religious Freedom Act is passed to give legal protection to the church's use of peyote
The Religious Freedom Restoration Act, with rulings such as US v. Boyll (1991), allows members to possess and use peyote for religious purposes

f.origin: The Oklahoma Territory (1890–1907) in the late nineteenth century, after peyote was introduced to the southern Great Plains from Mexico.
f.founder: none: it grew among Native American peoples of the southern Great Plains; figures named in its development include Chevato, Jim Aton, John Wilson, Jonathan Koshiway and Victor Griffin.
f.scriptures: none: ceremonies draw on prayer, peyote songs and drumming; the Cross-fire way also uses Bible readings, and the Half-Moon way uses no Bible.
f.followers: An estimated 300,000 adherents in the United States, Canada and Mexico.
